headline: Use three random words for passwords you must remember
technical: A password made of three random words, like 'tractor paper garden', is long, hard to guess and easy to remember. Length beats complexity: adding symbols to a short word helps far less than adding another word. Use a different one for every important account.
why: Most account takeovers start with a guessed or reused password.
scene: three glowing word blocks forming a key in front of a padlock

headline: Let a password manager remember your passwords
technical: A password manager creates a strong, unique password for every site and fills it in for you, so you only remember one master password. Most are built into your phone or browser already. Protect the master password with 2-step verification.
why: Reusing one password means one breach unlocks all your accounts.
scene: a glowing vault holding many small keys

headline: Turn on 2-step verification for your email first
technical: 2-step verification (2SV or MFA) asks for a second check, like a code or an app prompt, when someone signs in from a new device. Start with your email account, because it can reset the passwords of everything else. Then add it to banking, social media and shopping accounts.
why: Even if your password leaks, 2SV stops most attackers at the door.
scene: a smartphone showing a glowing approval shield beside a laptop login

headline: What are passkeys, and should you use them?
technical: A passkey replaces your password with a cryptographic key stored on your phone or computer, unlocked with your fingerprint, face or PIN. There is nothing to type, so there is nothing for a fake website to steal. Google, Apple, Microsoft and many shops now support them.
why: Passkeys can't be phished, which removes the most common attack.
scene: a fingerprint turning into a glowing key

headline: Got a scam text? Forward it to 7726
technical: In the UK you can forward suspicious texts to 7726 for free. Your mobile network uses the reports to block scam numbers for everyone. Don't click links in the message and don't reply.
why: Every report helps block the sender before they reach someone else.
scene: a smartphone with a suspicious message being sent into a glowing shield

headline: Forward scam emails to report@phishing.gov.uk
technical: The NCSC runs a free UK service that takes down scam websites reported by the public. Forward the suspicious email to report@phishing.gov.uk, then delete it. If you clicked a link or entered details, change that password and contact your bank if money is involved.
why: Reports have taken down hundreds of thousands of scam sites.
scene: an envelope with a fishing hook being caught by a glowing net

headline: Turn on automatic updates and stop delaying them
technical: Updates fix security holes that attackers already know about, often within days of a fix being released. Switch on automatic updates for your phone, computer, browser and apps. If a device no longer gets updates, it's time to replace it.
why: Unpatched software is one of the main ways devices get hacked.
scene: a laptop receiving a glowing download shield

headline: Back up the files you can't afford to lose
technical: Keep a copy of important photos and documents somewhere other than your device, like a cloud service or an external drive you unplug afterwards. Check now and then that you can actually restore a file. A backup you've never tested may not work when you need it.
why: Backups turn ransomware, theft or a broken phone into an inconvenience.
scene: a cloud and an external drive both holding glowing copies of folders

headline: The 3-2-1 backup rule, in one minute
technical: Keep 3 copies of important data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy offsite or offline. For businesses, the offline or immutable copy matters most, because ransomware gangs now hunt for and delete reachable backups first. Test restores regularly.
why: Backups the attacker can reach are backups the attacker can destroy.
scene: three glowing data cubes, one sealed in an offline vault

headline: Check if your email was in a data breach
technical: Have I Been Pwned is a free, trusted service that tells you which known breaches include your email address. If you appear in one, change that site's password and any account where you used the same one. You can also sign up to be alerted about future breaches.
why: Knowing what leaked tells you exactly what to change.
scene: a magnifying glass over an email envelope with glowing data fragments

headline: Run a 2-minute security check-up on your Google account
technical: Google's Security Checkup shows which devices are signed in, which apps can access your account, and whether recovery details are up to date. Remove anything you don't recognise. Apple and Microsoft accounts have similar pages in their settings.
why: Forgotten devices and old app access are easy ways in.
scene: a checklist with glowing ticks beside a shield

headline: Lost money to a scam? Act within the hour
technical: Call your bank straight away using the number on the back of your card, so they can try to stop or recover the payment. Then report it to Action Fraud, the UK's national reporting centre for fraud and cybercrime. Keep the messages, numbers and receipts as evidence.
why: Banks can often recover money only if they hear about it quickly.
scene: a bank card with a glowing shield and a clock

headline: Five signs a message is a phishing scam
technical: Watch for urgency ('act now or lose access'), requests for passwords or payment, a sender address that doesn't quite match, links that go somewhere unexpected, and offers that are too good to be true. If unsure, contact the company using a number or app you already trust, not the message.
why: Phishing is still the most common start of a cyber attack.
scene: a fishing hook pulling a password card out of an email

headline: Be careful with QR codes in emails and car parks
technical: Scammers now hide phishing links in QR codes, because email filters can't easily read them and phones show less of the link. Fake QR stickers on parking meters are a common UK trick. Check the web address after scanning and pay through the official app when you can.
why: A QR code is just a link you can't see before you open it.
scene: a QR code with a hidden fishing hook inside

headline: SIM swap fraud: how criminals steal your number
technical: In a SIM swap, a criminal convinces your mobile network to move your number to their SIM, then receives your text codes. Signs include suddenly losing signal. Ask your network about a PIN or extra checks, and use an authenticator app instead of SMS codes where you can.
why: Whoever holds your number can often reset your accounts.
scene: a SIM card being swapped between two phones with a warning glow

headline: Is public Wi-Fi safe to use?
technical: Most websites and apps now encrypt traffic, so everyday browsing on public Wi-Fi is far safer than it used to be. The bigger risk is fake hotspots with names like the café's. Use your mobile data for banking if unsure, and keep your device updated.
why: The network name can be faked; your phone's own data can't.
scene: a coffee cup beside a glowing wifi symbol with a shield

headline: Explainer: what is a zero-day?
technical: A zero-day is a security flaw that attackers know about before the vendor has a fix, so defenders have had 'zero days' to patch. Once a fix is released it's often called an n-day, and attacks usually increase as more criminals copy the exploit. That's why patching quickly after a zero-day fix matters.
why: Zero-days are rare but the window right after the fix is the most dangerous.
scene: a cracked shield with a glowing countdown at zero

headline: Explainer: CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list
technical: CISA, the US cyber agency, keeps a public list of vulnerabilities that attackers are actually using, not just theoretical ones. US federal agencies must patch them by a deadline, and many companies worldwide use it to decide what to fix first. CyberSid shows new entries as 'CISA Known Exploited'.
why: It's the best free signal for which patches can't wait.
scene: a glowing priority list with a red flag at the top

headline: Explainer: what does a CVSS score like 9.8 mean?
technical: CVSS rates how severe a vulnerability is from 0 to 10, based on things like whether it can be exploited remotely and without a login. 9.0 and above is Critical. But a score isn't the whole story: a 7.5 flaw being exploited today is more urgent than an unexploited 9.8.
why: Prioritise by real-world exploitation, not just the number.
scene: a glowing gauge pointing near maximum

headline: Explainer: MFA fatigue attacks
technical: Attackers who already have a password spam the victim with sign-in approval prompts, hoping they tap Approve just to make it stop, often late at night. Number matching, where you type a code shown on screen, defeats most of these. Never approve a prompt you didn't start.
why: Several major breaches started with one tired tap on Approve.
scene: a phone flooded with glowing approval pop-ups

headline: Explainer: phishing-resistant MFA
technical: Codes and push prompts can be stolen by fake login pages that pass them on in real time. Phishing-resistant methods like passkeys and FIDO2 security keys check the real website's address, so they simply won't work on a fake site. They're now recommended for admins and high-risk users.
why: It closes the gap that modern phishing kits exploit.
scene: a hardware security key plugged into a laptop with a shield

headline: Explainer: infostealer malware
technical: Infostealers are malware that quietly copies saved passwords, browser cookies and crypto wallets from a computer, then sells them in bulk. Stolen session cookies can let attackers skip passwords and MFA entirely. They often arrive through cracked software, fake game mods or malicious ads.
why: Many recent company breaches began with one infected personal laptop.
scene: a shadowy hand pulling glowing keys out of a laptop

headline: Explainer: business email compromise
technical: In business email compromise (BEC), criminals hijack or imitate a real email account, then ask for an urgent payment or changed bank details. There's often no malware at all, just a convincing message. Always confirm new or changed payment details by phone using a number you already have.
why: BEC causes bigger losses than ransomware in many years.
scene: an email with a fake invoice and a glowing pound sign

headline: Explainer: double extortion ransomware
technical: Modern ransomware gangs steal data before encrypting it, then threaten to publish it if the victim doesn't pay. So good backups alone no longer remove the pressure. Some groups now skip encryption completely and rely only on data theft.
why: It's why breaches and ransomware are now usually the same story.
scene: a locked server with data files escaping out of the side

headline: Explainer: living off the land
technical: 'Living off the land' means attackers use tools already built into the system, like PowerShell or remote management software, instead of bringing their own malware. Because the tools are legitimate, antivirus often doesn't flag them. Detecting it relies on spotting unusual behaviour.
why: It's how many state-backed groups stay hidden for months.
scene: a toolbox of glowing system tools being used by a shadow

headline: Explainer: supply chain attacks
technical: Instead of attacking a company directly, criminals compromise a supplier, software update or code library it trusts. One breach can then reach thousands of customers at once. Knowing which suppliers can access your systems is the first step to managing the risk.
why: Your security is only as strong as the weakest company you trust.
scene: a chain of glowing boxes with one cracked link

headline: How to read the CHAIN button on CyberSid cards
technical: The CHAIN view shows how an attack worked, step by step, using MITRE ATT&CK stages like Initial Access, Execution and Exfiltration. Each step links to the matching technique on MITRE's site. It helps defenders see where they could have broken the chain.
why: Stopping any one step can stop the whole attack.
scene: a chain of glowing links, each with a small icon

headline: Explainer: least privilege
technical: Least privilege means every person and system gets only the access they need, for only as long as they need it. Admin rights used for everyday work are a common way small incidents become big ones. Separate admin accounts and time-limited access reduce the damage of any single compromise.
why: Attackers inherit whatever access the account they steal has.
scene: a set of doors where only one glowing door is unlocked

headline: Explainer: Patch Tuesday
technical: Microsoft releases most of its security updates on the second Tuesday of each month, a schedule many other vendors follow. Attackers study the fixes to work out what was broken, so the days after Patch Tuesday are busy for both sides. Critical and exploited fixes should go out first.
why: Knowing the rhythm helps you plan patching instead of reacting.
scene: a calendar with the second Tuesday glowing

headline: Why firewalls and VPNs are top targets
technical: Firewalls, VPN gateways and email security appliances sit on the internet edge and are reachable by anyone. A single flaw can give direct access to the network, which is why vendors like Fortinet, Ivanti, Cisco and Palo Alto appear so often in exploited lists. Patch them first and limit who can reach their admin pages.
why: The device protecting the door is often the door itself.
scene: a glowing firewall wall with a small crack being probed

headline: Deepfake voice scams: agree a family safe word
technical: Criminals can clone a voice from a short online clip and call pretending to be a relative in trouble, asking for money urgently. Agree a simple safe word with close family that a real caller would know. If in doubt, hang up and call them back on their usual number.
why: A voice alone is no longer proof of who's calling.
scene: a phone with a glowing sound wave and a question mark

headline: Delete accounts you no longer use
technical: Old accounts on forums, shops and apps still hold your details, and often an old reused password. When those sites are breached, your data goes with them. Close what you don't need and change the password on anything you keep.
why: Every unused account is a breach waiting to include you.
scene: a stack of dusty account cards being swept away

headline: Five free security steps for small businesses
technical: Back up important data, protect devices from malware, keep phones and laptops updated, use strong passwords with 2-step verification, and teach staff to spot phishing. The NCSC's free Small Business Guide covers each one in plain English.
why: Most attacks on small firms are opportunistic and blocked by the basics.
scene: a small shop front protected by a glowing shield

headline: Check which apps can see your location and photos
technical: Apps often ask for more access than they need. On Android, go to Settings then Privacy to review permissions; on iPhone, Settings then Privacy & Security. Switch off access an app doesn't need, and remove apps you no longer use.
why: Less access means less to leak if an app is compromised.
scene: a phone with app icons behind glowing permission locks

headline: Use a screen lock and turn on Find My Device
technical: A PIN, fingerprint or face lock stops a lost phone becoming an open door to your email and banking. Turn on Find My Device (Android) or Find My (iPhone) so you can locate or wipe it remotely. Set this up before you need it.
why: A lost unlocked phone gives access to almost everything.
scene: a smartphone with a glowing padlock and a location pin

headline: Think you've been hacked? The first three steps
technical: First, change the password of the affected account from a different, clean device, and sign out other sessions. Second, turn on or reset 2-step verification and check recovery email and phone haven't been changed. Third, warn contacts if messages were sent from your account, and report fraud if money is involved.
why: Acting fast stops one compromised account spreading to others.
scene: a glowing checklist with three steps beside a shield

headline: Lost money to online fraud? Call 1930 straight away
technical: In India, call the national cybercrime helpline 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in as soon as you notice. Reporting within the first hours gives banks the best chance to hold the money before it is moved on. Keep screenshots, transaction IDs and the fraudster's numbers as evidence.
why: The faster you report, the more likely the money can still be stopped.
scene: a smartphone showing a glowing emergency call button beside a frozen stack of coins

headline: 'Digital arrest' is always a scam
technical: Fraudsters pose as police, CBI, customs or courier staff on video calls, claim a parcel or your Aadhaar is linked to a crime, and keep you 'under digital arrest' until you pay. No Indian agency arrests anyone over a video call or asks for money to clear your name. Hang up and call 1930.
why: People have lost their life savings to this script.
scene: a laptop video call screen with a fake police badge and a padlock breaking apart

headline: You never need your UPI PIN to receive money
technical: Scammers send collect requests or QR codes and say you will receive a refund or prize once you enter your PIN. Entering your UPI PIN only ever sends money out of your account. Check every request carefully and decline any you don't recognise.
why: One wrong PIN entry can empty an account in seconds.
scene: a phone payment screen with a glowing PIN pad and a warning shield

headline: Report fraud calls and messages on Sanchar Saathi
technical: The government's Sanchar Saathi portal and app has a Chakshu feature for reporting suspected fraud calls, SMS and WhatsApp messages, such as fake KYC, prize or electricity bill messages. Reports help telecom operators and authorities block the numbers and links involved.
why: Every report helps block a scammer before they reach the next person.
scene: a smartphone with a flagged suspicious message and a shield blocking it

headline: Check how many SIM cards are registered in your name
technical: On Sanchar Saathi you can see every mobile connection linked to your identity and report any you don't recognise. Criminals use SIM cards taken out in other people's names to run scams, so an unknown number in your name is worth reporting straight away.
why: A SIM in your name could be used for crimes you know nothing about.
scene: several glowing SIM cards on a table with one marked by a red warning light

headline: Lost your phone? Block it through CEIR
technical: If your phone is lost or stolen, file a police report, then use the CEIR service on Sanchar Saathi to block its IMEI so it can't be used on Indian mobile networks. If you get the phone back, you can unblock it through the same service.
why: A blocked phone is far less useful to a thief.
scene: a smartphone locked inside a glowing shield with a network signal crossed out

headline: Lock your Aadhaar biometrics when you don't need them
technical: UIDAI lets you lock your Aadhaar biometrics on the myAadhaar website or the mAadhaar app, so your fingerprints can't be used for authentication until you unlock them. It helps protect against fraud that uses cloned fingerprints to withdraw money through Aadhaar-enabled payments.
why: Cloned fingerprints have been used to drain bank accounts without any OTP.
scene: a glowing fingerprint inside a padlock above an identity card

headline: Banks don't ask you to update KYC through an SMS link
technical: Messages saying your account or SIM will be blocked unless you update KYC through a link are a common scam. Banks never ask for your OTP, PIN or password. Don't click; open your bank's official app or visit the branch yourself if you're unsure.
why: The link leads to a fake page that steals your banking details.
scene: a phone showing an urgent message with a fishing hook hanging over a bank icon

headline: Paid to like videos? It's a task scam
technical: Messages on WhatsApp or Telegram offer easy money for liking videos or rating hotels. You get small payments at first, then you're asked to 'invest' to unlock bigger tasks, and the money disappears. Genuine jobs never ask you to pay to work. Report it at cybercrime.gov.in.
why: The first small payments are bait to win your trust.
scene: a phone with thumbs-up icons turning into a trap closing on a coin

headline: Explainer: reporting cyber incidents to CERT-In
technical: Under CERT-In's 2022 directions, organisations in India must report certain cyber incidents, such as ransomware, data breaches and website defacements, to CERT-In within six hours of noticing them. Keep the reporting contact and an internal process ready before you need them.
why: Six hours passes very quickly in the middle of an incident.
scene: a server room with a glowing stopwatch and an alert beacon

headline: Fake loan apps: check the lender before you borrow
technical: Illegal loan apps offer instant loans, then copy your contacts and photos and harass you and your family to repay far more. Before borrowing, check that the lender is a bank or an RBI-registered NBFC, never give a loan app access to your contacts, and report illegal lenders on RBI's Sachet portal.
why: Harassment by illegal loan apps has ruined lives.
scene: a smartphone loan app with chains around a contact list
